title: Largest Set Intersection

description.intro: You are given a non-empty array, sets, where each element is an array of unique integers representing a set. The intersection of a list of sets is the set of elements that appears in every set. Return the index of the set that should be excluded to maximize the size of the intersection of the remaining sets. In case of a tie, return the smallest index.
examples:
Example 1: sets = [[1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1], [1, 4, 5], [1, 2]]
Output: 2
Explanation: Excluding the third set (index 2)
yields a set intersection of size 2: {1, 2}.

Example 2: sets = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
Output: 0
Explanation: The sets don't have any elements in common,
so the intersection will be empty regardless of which set you exclude.

Example 3: sets = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]]
Output: 1
Explanation: After excluding a set, there will be only one set left,
so the intersection is the remaining set.

Example 4: sets = [[1, 2, 3]]
Output: 0
Explanation: There is only one set, so after excluding it,
the intersection is empty.
description.approach:
1 ≤ sets.length ≤ 10^5
0 ≤ sets[i].length ≤ 10^5
The total number of elements across all sets is at most 10^5
All integers in each set are unique
-10^9 ≤ sets[i][j] ≤ 10^9

Frequency Map solution
Let's start with an easier problem: computing the intersection of a (non-empty) list of sets. If the lists have n elements in total, this can be done in O(n) time, assuming all the sets are hash sets.

A naive solution would be to consider excluding the sets one by one and call set_intersection() for the remaining sets. This would take O(k*n) time, where k is the number of sets.

We should hunt for properties we can leverage. First, let's ignore the edge cases with only one or two sets -- if there's only one set, the answer is 0, and if there are two, the answer is the largest of the two.

If we focus on a specific number, x, what can we say about it? We can do a case analysis:

If x appears in every set, it will be in the intersection regardless of our choice, so we don't need to factor such elements in our choice.
If x appears in only one set, it won't be in the intersection regardless of our choice, because we must include at least one set without it. In fact, any element that appears less than k-1 times won't be in the intersection and can be ignored.
This only leaves numbers that are missing from exactly one set, i.e., that appear k-1 times. If x is missing from exactly one set, x will only be in the intersection if we pick that set.
This means we want to pick the set with the fewest elements that appear in k-1 sets. We can turn this thought into an algorithm:

Create a frequency map from integers to the number of sets they appear in.
For each set, count how many elements it has with a frequency of k-1.
Return the index of the set with the smallest count.

complexity:
Time & Space Analysis
n: total number of elements across all sets
k: number of sets
Frequency Map solution:

Time: O(n) - we make a single pass through all elements to build the frequency map, and then another pass through all elements to count those that appear k-1 times.
Extra space: O(n) - we store at most n elements in the frequency map.
Prefix Sum solution:

Time: O(n)
Extra space: O(n)
The worst case is when the sets have as many repeated elements as possible. Otherwise, the size of the prefix/suffix intersections quickly collapses.

So, imagine that we have O(sqrt(n)) sets, each with the exact same O(sqrt(n)) elements.

We'll spend O(sqrt(n)) to compute each prefix/suffix intersection. We'll then spend O(sqrt(n)) to compute the intersection of each prefix/suffix with the next/previous prefix/suffix. In total, we do O(sqrt(n) * sqrt(n)) = O(n) work.

def run_tests():
  tests = [
      # Example 1 
      ([[1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 1], [1, 4, 5], [1, 2]], 2),
      # Example 2 
      ([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], 0),
      # Example 3 
      ([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]], 1),
      # Example 4 
      ([[1, 2, 3]], 0),
      # Additional test cases
      ([[1], [1]], 0),
      ([[1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 3]], 0),
  ]
  for sets, want in tests:
    got_freq = largest_set_intersection_frequency_map(sets)
    got_prefix = largest_set_intersection_prefix_sum(sets)
    assert got_freq == want, f"\nlargest_set_intersection_frequency_map({sets}): got: {got_freq}, want: {want}\n"
    assert got_prefix == want, f"\nlargest_set_intersection_prefix_sum({sets}): got: {got_prefix}, want: {want}\n"

run_tests()
